children.text: A trip from the UK to Egypt is, for its distance, easy to assemble. From London to
Cairo
, and from several UK airports to Sharm el-Sheikh or
Hurghada

, direct flights run in some seasons and on some routes. The flight time is generally longer than a short European break and shorter than a long-haul Asia or Americas trip. Egypt's strength sits in between.
Egypt is not a single holiday product. Cairo and
Giza
Luxor
and
Aswan

, Red Sea resorts, Sinai, the Western Desert — the airport you need, the trip's pace, and the standard of satisfaction all change. With more options out of the UK, the first decision is "which Egypt are you going to?"
Airport choice decides the trip

Cairo International is the doorway for ancient sites and city culture. To see the Giza pyramids, the Grand Egyptian Museum, Saqqara, the Islamic quarter, and the Coptic quarter, starting in Cairo is natural. Domestic connections to Luxor and Aswan are many; for a cultural trip, it is the easiest starting airport.
Luxor International suits travellers whose main goal is ancient Egypt. Karnak,
Luxor Temple
, the
Valley of the Kings
, the Hatshepsut mortuary temple, and
Medinet Habu
cluster close together. UK direct flights are fewer than to Cairo or the Red Sea resorts; depending on season, a Cairo connection becomes the answer.

Sharm el-Sheikh sits on the southern tip of Sinai as a Red Sea resort. Ras Mohammed, the Strait of Tiran, wreck diving, winter sun, and resort time. Leisure routes from UK regional airports are abundant; for a sea-focused traveller, a legible choice.

Hurghada is the mainland Red Sea base. Many all-inclusive hotels, useful for family travel, winter beach, diving, and snorkelling. A major advantage is pairing with Luxor. The road is about three and a half to four hours each way; for travellers who want the Red Sea and the ancient sites in one trip, it is practical.
Aswan is unusual as a starting airport. For travellers focused on Philae, Nubian culture, the Nile islands, and
Abu Simbel
access, it has value. UK direct connections are limited; you'll usually meet Aswan inside a Cairo, Luxor, or Nile cruise flow.
How to think about flights

To Cairo from the UK, London Heathrow direct flights are the base. From Cairo, domestic flights link Luxor, Aswan, Hurghada, and Sharm el-Sheikh. For multi-city trips, using Cairo as the hub organises best.
To the Red Sea resorts, seasonal and leisure flights run from London and from Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, and Glasgow. TUI, easyJet, and Jet2 routes are convenient for a seaside package.

When comparing flights, look at the arrival destination, not only the price. A Cairo trip, a Hurghada trip, and a Sharm trip are practically different trips inside the same "Egypt." A cheap flight is not necessarily the right one for your purpose.
Visa and entry

A UK passport for tourism in Egypt typically needs a visa. GOV.UK notes that a 30-day visa can be purchased at kiosks at approved arrival airports; an online e-visa is also available. Conditions and fees change, so check GOV.UK and Egypt's official e-visa portal before travelling.
Passports need at least six months remaining beyond the arrival date, and blank pages. Airlines check at check-in; don't run close to the edge.

For stays only in Sinai (such as Sharm el-Sheikh) under fifteen days without onward travel to the mainland, a different entry treatment may apply. Adding Cairo, Luxor, Hurghada, or Aswan means a standard Egyptian visa. Don't conflate a short Sinai-only resort stay with a trip that includes mainland Egypt.
When to go

For ancient sites and the Nile, October to April is easiest. Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan all walk well and you can start sites in the morning. November and February balance climate, light, crowds, and price.

December to January is comfortable; UK winter demand and international peak overlap. Lock in good hotels, Nile cruises, guides, and domestic flights early. The Valley of the Kings and Karnak crowd later in the day.

May to September is very hot in upper Egypt. Luxor and Aswan daytime sightseeing wants stamina. For summer trips, early-morning, midday rest, late-afternoon-out is the realistic design. Prices can drop; underestimating the heat drops the trip's quality.

The Red Sea runs year-round. Winter suits UK sun-seeking trips; summer warms the water. Midsummer Hurghada or Sharm is hot, and time inside the resort dominates. A seaside trip and a Luxor sites trip feel different even in the same season.
Decide the trip type
UK Egypt trips split into three. A Red Sea beach holiday; an ancient-Egypt tour; or a combination.

Red Sea–only, build around Sharm el-Sheikh or Hurghada. Hotel, sea, pool, diving, snorkelling, desert tours. Legible, and works well as a UK winter escape. Staying only inside the resort area, you barely touch Egyptian cities or history. Fine if that is the goal; if you also want pyramids and temples, it falls short.

For ancient Egypt as the main goal, Cairo, Giza, Saqqara, Luxor, Aswan, and Abu Simbel are the base. Eight days minimum, ideally ten or more, reduces strain. Giza and the GEM alone consume time; Luxor isn't enough in a day.

The highest-satisfaction shape tends to be history first, sea-rest last. Enter via Cairo, run through Luxor and Aswan, close with Hurghada or Sharm. Reverse works; after relaxing at the beach, early starts and site days are surprisingly tiring.
Cairo and Giza

If you enter via Cairo, don't end with the Giza pyramids only. Adding Saqqara's step pyramid, the Pyramid Texts inside Unas, and the memory of Memphis lets Giza appear as the culmination of a long architectural experiment rather than a sudden miracle.

The Grand Egyptian Museum has made a Giza stay weightier than before. Tutankhamun's funerary equipment, colossal sculpture, and dynastic objects are close to the pyramids. On a first trip, don't cram the plateau and the museum into one day; protect stamina and concentration.
Inside Cairo, the Islamic and Coptic quarters matter.
Khan el-Khalili
, al-Muizz Street, the
Mosque of Ibn Tulun
the Hanging Church
, the Church of St. Sergius, and
the Coptic Museum
show that Egypt is not built only out of the pharaonic period.
Luxor and Aswan
Luxor is the centre of an Egypt trip. East-bank Karnak and Luxor Temple; west-bank Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut, Medinet Habu,
the Ramesseum
, Deir el-Medina. The east is the temple-and-city side; the west is the landscape of tombs and rebirth. Holding the split in mind deepens the visit.

In the Valley of the Kings, choose tombs rather than entering all. Tutankhamun, Seti I, Ramses V and VI often need separate tickets; choose by time, crowds, preservation, and stamina. Here, explanation quality maps directly to experience. The wall paintings are not only beautiful; they are a practical religious map for the dead to cross the night into rebirth.

Aswan is quieter than Luxor and slows the trip. Philae, the Unfinished Obelisk, the Nubian Museum, the Nile islands, and the granite landscape of the first cataract show a different Egypt from Cairo and Luxor. For Abu Simbel, don't reduce Aswan to a stop.
The Nile cruise

A Nile cruise between Luxor and Aswan is a classic shape that UK travellers find legible. Edfu, Kom Ombo, and Esna — places hard to put together independently — fit naturally into the boat's flow. Not changing hotels each day, it works well on a first circuit.
Large boats are efficient; time is fixed. Sightseeing, meals, disembarkation, and transfers follow the boat. Good for short trips; not the same as a quiet river trip.

For slower, a dahabiya is worth considering. A small sailing-style cruise with longer time and, on some boats, smaller villages and quiet moorings. Higher price, fewer cabins; for travellers who want to change the speed at which they see the Nile, it fits.
The Red Sea
The Red Sea trip is the most casual shape of UK Egypt travel. Winter sun, sea, hotel, pool, diving, snorkelling. With a clear purpose, it works very well.

Sharm el-Sheikh has strong marine environment. Ras Mohammed, the Strait of Tiran, wreck diving, and Sinai mountain views appeal. For diving priority, look beyond hotel price at the dive centre, boat quality, and distance to sites.

Hurghada is larger and easier for families. Including El Gouna, Soma Bay, and Sahl Hasheesh, the atmosphere of the stay shifts considerably. To combine with Luxor, Hurghada is often easier than Sharm.

St. Catherine's Monastery and Mount Sinai as day trips or one-night trips from Sharm are an option some travellers consider; confirm access status close to the visit. Sinai's interior is not to be treated with the same feel as the Red Sea coast.
Cost and cash

Egypt is a cost-effective country for UK travellers. Food, transfers, lodging, and services are often more reasonable than the UK or Western Europe. International flights, good hotels, Nile cruises, quality guides, and supplementary tickets are separate. Treating the country as cheap drops the trip's quality.

Cash is needed. Tipping, small shops, markets, short transfers, restrooms, and local eateries take Egyptian-pound small notes. Cards work at hotels and large restaurants; don't plan everything as card-based.

Tipping is hard to avoid in Egypt. You don't need to respond to every request. Guides, drivers, hotel staff, and boat crew — people who really support the trip — earn a tip you should build into the budget.
Safety and practical notes

UK travellers should check the FCDO advice for Egypt before booking and before departure. Cairo, Giza, Luxor, Aswan, Hurghada, and Sharm el-Sheikh are standard tourism routes; North Sinai, the Libyan border area, and parts of the desert receive different treatment.

In-city movement stabilises with trusted transfers, hotel arrangements, and ride-hailing. Cairo traffic is heavy; airport and Giza transfer times vary considerably by hour. On a domestic-flight day, don't cut the transfer too close.

Split dress between Red Sea resort and city/religious sites. At the hotel pool and beach, resort feel is fine; at mosques, churches, markets, and provincial towns, don't expose shoulders or knees significantly. At sites, walking shoes, hat, and sunglasses are needed.

Don't drink tap water; use bottled. For sensitive stomachs, be cautious with ice, raw vegetables, and street food. In summer or upper Egypt, don't underestimate dehydration. Sites have little shade in places.
Why the UK trip is worth it
UK to Egypt is neither too close nor too far. It can be a casual winter beach trip or a serious ancient-sites trip. The problem is the two are easily sold as the same thing.

A Red Sea rest trip is valuable in itself. A Cairo–Luxor tour is valuable in itself. Combining the two needs days and order. Rather than cramming everything into a short holiday, deciding what plays the lead lets Egypt read better.

The pyramids are larger than the photographs. Luxor is deeper than a day. The Red Sea spreads beyond the hotel pool. The distance from the UK is right. Treat the trip too easily and you'll miss what is there.

deck: A practical guide for travellers planning Egypt from the UK — direct flights, airport choice, visa, season, and how to combine the Red Sea and ancient sites.
